title: Draw every elimination product
asks: A halide (or dihalide) is treated with base. Draw all the products.

know.h: An elimination removes the leaving group and one hydrogen from a carbon next to it (a beta carbon). The C=C forms between those two carbons.
Each different beta carbon that has a hydrogen gives a different alkene (regioisomers). Beta carbons that are equivalent by symmetry give the same alkene, so count it once.
A beta carbon with no hydrogen gives nothing. A halide with no beta hydrogen at all (methyl, or {{(CH3)3CCH2Br}}) cannot eliminate.
E and Z. A C=C has two geometric isomers when each of its carbons carries two different groups. If either carbon carries two identical groups (two H, or two {{CH3}}), there is only one alkene.
The lecture example: 2-bromo-3-methylpentane with {{NaOCH2CH3}} gives three alkenes, 3-methyl-1-pentene and the two geometric isomers of 3-methyl-2-pentene.
In a six-membered ring the C=C can only be cis, so a ring alkene has no E and Z pair. A double bond from a ring carbon to an outside carbon (exocyclic) is a separate regioisomer.
Two equivalents of strong base with a dihalide means two {{E2}} reactions: HX is lost twice and the products have two pi bonds. The formula drops by 2 HX: {{C4H8Br2}} gives {{C4H6}}.
Three kinds of product with two pi bonds: an alkyne (C≡C), a cumulated diene or allene (C=C=C), and a conjugated diene (C=C-C=C).

The second elimination starts from a bromoalkene. The hydrogen again comes from a carbon next to the C-Br carbon. If that hydrogen is on the alkene carbon, the product is an alkyne (Br on the double bond) or an allene (Br next to the double bond).
Different routes can end at the same product. In the exam question 1,2-butadiene forms from both bromoalkenes. Draw each product once.
Which is major, if asked: the more substituted alkene (Saytzeff), and E rather than Z, because the two larger groups are farther apart.

One stereoisomer, one geometry. When the beta carbon has only one hydrogen and both carbons are stereocentres, the anti-periplanar requirement allows only one of E or Z. A beta {{CH2}} has two hydrogens, so both E and Z can form from it.
Skill: be systematic. Work through the beta carbons in order and name or number each product so that duplicates are easy to spot.

method: Circle the carbon with the leaving group and mark every carbon next to it. Cross out any that has no hydrogen.
For each marked carbon, remove one of its hydrogens and the leaving group and draw the C=C. Drop duplicates that come from symmetry.
Test each alkene for E and Z: does each alkene carbon carry two different groups? If yes, draw both isomers.
With a dihalide and two equivalents of base, the alkenes from the first round still carry a halogen. Repeat the first three steps on each of them.
Collect the products, draw each once, and check the formula (one HX lost per elimination).
If the question asks, mark the major product: the most substituted alkene, E over Z.

pitfalls.h: Forgetting that an alkene such as 2-pentene is two compounds, E and Z.
Drawing E and Z for an alkene that has two identical groups on one carbon, such as 2-methyl-2-butene.
Missing a beta carbon, most often a {{CH3}} branch on the carbon that carries the leaving group.
Stopping after one elimination when the question gives two equivalents of base.
Leaving out the allene, or counting the same product twice because it was reached by two routes.
Making a double bond to a carbon that is not next to the leaving group.
